text: . lygerzeroOzero - 2y ago - Edited 2y ago 8 Top 1% Commenter It's a quirk of the fact that we use base 10 (that is, each digit is a multiple of 10). There's nothing inherently special about 10, we humans just decided on it because it makes it easy to count on our fingers. Edit: Base ten, as in twice five, because people on Reddit will be needlessly pedantic about everything. The digit sum truck for 9 works because 10 is exactly 9 > Let's look at the number 63. We can write 63 as: 6x10+3. Since 10 is exactly 9 + 1, we can rewrite this as: 6x(9+1)+3 Expand that and we get 6Xx9+6+3 The 6 x 9 part, aside from being nice, is obviously divisible by 9, so we can ignore it. That leaves the 6 + 3 part, which is the digit sum. If that part is also divisible by 9, then our original number must also be divisible by 9l To recap: we broke the original number down into two parts: a part that must be divisible by 9, (because it's just some number times 9) and the digit sum. So when the digit sum is also divisible by 9, we know the whole number must be. This works for any two digit number, and it turns out it also works for any bigger number too. We can write any number expanded out as a sum of powers of ten, so 1431 is just: 1x1000+4x100+3x10+1 And those powers of 10 can be written as 9 + 1 1000=10x10x10=(9+1)x (9+1)x (9+1) When you multiply that out, you always get a bunch of stuff times 9, plus a 1 at the end. And then plug that into our number expression, and we find: 1431 =(abunchof crap) x 9 +1+4+3+1 So obviously all the crap times 9 at the start must be divisible by 9. So we only need to check the last bit, which is the digit sum! You can basically do the same process to see why this is also true for 3, noting that 9 is not coincidentally 3 x 3. [e) 360
